articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities Supporting Hizballah's Financial Networks
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has imposed sanctions on three individuals and three entities for their roles in supporting Hizballah's financial activities. The designated individuals, Afif Abdel Rida Chouman, Hassan Khechen, and Ibrahim Khechen, are based in Lebanon.

The entities sanctioned include Wa Ta'awanu Association and Gold Global Company, both located in Lebanon, and Sankari Gold Kuyumculuk Ticaret Limited Sirketi in Turkey. These designations target a network involved in gold and cash smuggling, as well as a charity, all linked to Hizballah and the IRGC-QF.

These actions fall under Executive Order 13224, as amended, which targets terrorists and those who provide support to terrorists or acts of terrorism. U.S. persons are generally prohibited from engaging in transactions with these blocked persons, and foreign financial institutions facilitating significant transactions for these targets may face secondary sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Targets Guatemalan Drug Trafficking Organizations with Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has designated several drug trafficking organizations for their involvement in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. The entities added to OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List include LOS LORENZANAS (also known as LORENZANA DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATION, 'THE LORENZANA CLAN', and 'THE LORENZANA FAMILY'), based in Guatemala.

Also designated were LOS MENDOZA DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATION, operating across Guatemala, Honduras, and Belize, and LOS HUISTAS DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATION, located in Santa Ana Huista, Huehuetenango, and La Democracia, Huehuetenango, Guatemala. These organizations are identified as criminal organizations with links to Mexican narco-terrorist cartels such as the Sinaloa Cartel and Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generacion.

These designations carry secondary sanctions risk under section 1(b) of Executive Order 13224, as amended by Executive Order 13886, and fall under the Global Terrorism Sanctions Regulations and Executive Order 14059 related to illicit drugs.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation Information
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an update regarding Iran designations. This action is part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to maintain and enforce sanctions against entities and individuals involved in activities that contravene U.S. foreign policy objectives concerning Iran.

Further details on the specific entities or individuals affected by this update were not immediately released in the initial announcement, but such updates typically involve modifications to existing listings on the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List or other sanctions lists.
These updates are crucial for ensuring the accuracy and effectiveness of sanctions programs and require vigilance from financial institutions and businesses to remain compliant.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Iran-Related Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations. These actions are part of a broader strategy to counter the Iranian regime's destabilizing activities and its support for terrorism and proliferation.

The specific individuals or entities targeted by these designations were not detailed in the initial release, but such measures typically aim to disrupt financial networks and procurement efforts that benefit the Iranian government or its proxies.
These designations underscore the U.S. commitment to enforcing sanctions against Iran and highlight the continued risks for those engaging in transactions with sanctioned parties.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Cyber-related, Transnational Criminal Organizations, and Cuba Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a series of designations targeting cyber-related activities, transnational criminal organizations, and entities linked to Cuba. This multi-faceted action aims to disrupt illicit financial networks and address threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy.

In addition to the designations, OFAC also published a Cuba-related determination, providing further guidance or clarification on existing sanctions pertaining to the country. The specifics of this determination were not immediately available but are expected to impact transactions and interactions with Cuba.

These designations highlight the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to combat a range of illicit activities, from cybercrime to the financial support of authoritarian regimes, and emphasize the importance of robust compliance measures for all regulated entities.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Alert, Amends Venezuela GL, and Updates Listings
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has taken several significant actions, including publishing an Iran-related Alert titled 'Iranian Shadow Fleet Reliance on False Flags for Sanctions Evasion.' This alert aims to raise awareness about deceptive shipping practices used by Iran to circumvent sanctions.

Concurrently, OFAC issued Venezuela-related General License 5AA, which authorizes certain transactions related to the Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. 2020 8.5 Percent Bond on or after December 18, 2026. An amended Frequently Asked Question, FAQ 595, was also released to provide further clarity.

Additionally, OFAC made changes to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List and the Sectoral Sanctions Identifications (SSI) List, including new Iran-related designations and updates to certain Iran-related listings. These updates include individuals and entities primarily from India, Russia, and Iran, connected to shipping, financial services, and air transport.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License FF-1
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Iran General License FF-1, titled 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance.' This amended general license provides specific authorization for certain wind-down activities.

General Licenses are issued by OFAC to authorize categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs. This particular amendment indicates a specific period or set of conditions under which transactions related to the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance are permitted to conclude.

The issuance of such an amended license is a routine part of sanctions administration, allowing for orderly disengagement from sanctioned entities or activities while maintaining the overall integrity of the sanctions regime.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals for North Korea and DRC-Related Activities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in activities related to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions aim to disrupt illicit networks supporting both regimes.

Among the North Korea-related designations, OFAC added 'FIRST FINANCIAL AND TECHNICAL DEVELOPMENT CENTER', located in North Korea and Vladivostok, Russia, to its SDN List. Several individuals, including Ilya Aleksandrovich Boykov, Han Yu Song, and Ri Thae Chol, all with ties to Russia and North Korea, were also designated for their involvement in DPRK IT worker fraud targeting U.S. businesses.

The DRC-related designations were made in response to Rwanda's destabilizing activities in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, with the Treasury sanctioning the Rwandan Ministry of Defence and a financial institution supporting M23. These measures underscore the U.S. commitment to addressing human rights abuses and illicit financial activities globally.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Settles with OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement with Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-headquartered cloud networking solutions provider, for $1,529,685. The settlement resolves nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and related services to Joint Stock Company (JSC) Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA was blocked by operation of law due to being majority-owned by designated JSC Concern Almaz Antey.

OFAC determined that these violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious. The case highlights the importance of thorough due diligence, especially in acquisitions, to identify and address sanctions risks associated with acquired customer contracts and beneficial ownership.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Frequently Asked Questions on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has amended several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) as part of its ongoing review to ensure published guidance remains current. This update specifically addresses FAQ topics on Blocking and Rejecting Transactions and on Filing Reports with OFAC.

The revised FAQs (numbers 10, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53) clarify when financial institutions must freeze funds (block) versus returning them (reject), the interest blocked funds must earn, and whether service charges can be deducted from blocked accounts. They also explain notification requirements for customers, account openings involving blocked persons, and the timing and procedures for reporting blocked property and rejected transactions.

While these amendments do not introduce new sanctions programs or designations, they provide crucial clarifications for compliance teams, emphasizing the importance of correctly handling sanctions hits and adhering to reporting obligations.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Pays $1,529,685 for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations. The violations involved nine instances of exporting networking equipment and services to a Russian defense manufacturer, JSC Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), which was blocked by operation of law.

The violations occurred between September 2018 and March 2022. MMZA was majority-owned by JSC Concern Almaz Antey, a designated entity, making MMZA a blocked person even before its independent designation in June 2022.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious. This case highlights the importance of robust due diligence, especially when acquiring customer contracts, to identify and mitigate sanctions risks.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
